subject: trade off between n_eff and warmup (or, Stan with many cores)

messages.author: 17d9c7a6e1a581b8
messages.subject: trade off between n_eff and warmup (or, Stan with many cores)
parts:
Hi stan-users,

I have a large logistic regression model with many observations and many
covariates. Stan takes a very long time to fit. I am wondering to what extent
I can benefit from doing sampling in parallel and combining the samples.
Computers with lots of cores (>24) are becoming more common. Is there an good
way to think about the trade off between warmup period and the number of
effective samples when using NUTS(diag_e)?

For example, I'm noticing the number of effective samples seems to be moderately
lower with (1) than with (2) even though the "total post-warmup draws" are the
same:

(1) fit1 = model.sampling(data=schools_dat, chains=40, iter=200)
(2) fit2 = model.sampling(data=schools_dat, chains=4, iter=2000)

Thanks,

Allen

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] trade off between n_eff and warmup (or, Stan with many cores)
parts:
It's important to make sure you are drawing a sample from the proper
posterior, so it's critical to run enough warmup iterations for

* convergence of the parameters to the high volume mass of
the posterior, and

* convergence of the mass matrix and step size to values that'll
let you explore the posterior.

Then you can sample in parallel with full efficiency and it won't matter
how you distribute the sampling.

The problem is then that your total runtime is bounded below by convergence
time on a single chain on a single processor. But that number is highly
variable given seed (and hence randomization in inits and iterations),
so Andrew's been encouraging us to think about a time-based scheme where we
run K parallel chains, each for Tw units of time for warmup and Ts units of
time for sampling. Then we can somehow downweight the chains that have not
converged because they'll have fewer iterations --- it requires a ragged R-hat
or something like it to do convergence monitoring --- I don't know enough
about Ben's scheme to know if it'd work.

But some problems converge pretty quickly, and in those cases, you can
really benefit from parallelization already. For example, suppose you
converge in 200 warmup iterations, have an n_eff rate of 1 per 2 iterations
and you need an n_eff of 1000. Then rather than running 200 + 2000 in a single
chain (I know, Andrew, we'd never ever ever do that, now back to our program),
you can 20 instances of 200 warmup + 100 sampling, and it only takes 1/5 the total time
(assuming there's some time for merging and warmup iterations are slower than sampling).

It also looks like we are going to need to concentrate more on convergence time!
Anyone want to come up with a clever parallel algorithm for that? Or maybe something
stochastic on the data that might converge more quickly than a batch algorithm?

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] trade off between n_eff and warmup (or, Stan with many cores)
parts:
Warmup is a tricky beast.  Technically if everything is well-behaved then the
convergence time should be on the order of the autocorrelation time of the
chain, so it should only take a few effective samples worth of iterations before
you can transition into sampling.

The bigger issue for us is adaptation.  100 samples isn’t quite enough to learn
the mass matrix particularly well so you’ll have lots of poorly-tuned chains.
Really what you’d want to do is the “couple all chains in warmup by having
them pool covariance estimates” but we’re not there yet internally.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] trade off between n_eff and warmup (or, Stan with many cores)
parts:
On Sunday, November 2, 2014 6:38:18 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
This reminds me, I want to see the definition of B-hat!

There are about 30 posts about it on stan-dev over the past year. If you prefer, you can define it as the square root of

[ (N - 1) / N * W + B / N ] / W

with a different way of calculating W and B, although I had previously been defining it just as F = B / W. Either way, it isn't especially interpretable as a loss function, but you can get a p-value via a permutation test that randomly scrambles the chain-time structure of the output iff you can first thin the chains so that the draws are exchangeable within-chain, which is where all the controversy starts.

Ben
